question.text: Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if \[ f_x(x,y) = axy-5y^2, \qquad f_y(x,y) = x^2-bxy. \]
question.explanation:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives: \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( f_x(x,y) \big) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( axy-5y^2 \big) \\[3pt] &= ax-10y \\[7pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( f_y(x,y) \big)\\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( x^2-bxy \big)\\[3pt] &= 2x-by \end{align*}

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

\begin{align*} ax-10y = 2x-by. \end{align*}

Equating the coefficients of $x$ and $y,$ respectively, we see that $a=2$ and $b=10.$

question.text: Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if \[ f_x(x,y) = y(1+x)e^x+axy^3+3x^2, \qquad f_y(x,y) = bxe^x-3x^2y^2. \]
question.explanation:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives: \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( f_x(x,y) \big) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big(y(1+x)e^x+axy^3+3x^2 \big) \\[3pt] &= (1+x)e^x+3axy^2+ 0 \\[3pt] &= (1+x)e^x+3axy^2 \\[7pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( f_y(x,y) \big)\\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( bxe^x-3x^2y^2 \big)\\[3pt] &= b(1+x)e^x-6xy^2 \end{align*}

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

\begin{align*} (1+x)e^x+3axy^2 = b(1+x)e^x-6xy^2 . \end{align*}

Equating the coefficients of $(1+x)e^x$ and $xy^2,$ respectively, we see that $b=1$ and $a=-2.$

question.text: Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if \begin{align} f_x(x,y) &= ax^2y^2+6xy+2x, \\[5pt] f_y(x,y) &= bx^3y+3x^2+2, \\[5pt] f_y(-1,1) &= 3. \end{align}
question.explanation:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives: \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( f_x(x,y) \big) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( ax^2y^2+6xy+2x \big) \\[3pt] &= 2ax^2y + 6x + 0 \\[3pt] &= 2ax^2y + 6x \\[7pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( f_y(x,y) \big)\\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( bx^3y+3x^2+2 \big)\\[3pt] &= 3bx^2y + 6x + 0 \\[3pt] &= 3bx^2y+6x \end{align*}

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

\begin{align*} 2ax^2y + 6x = 3bx^2y+6x. \end{align*}

Equating the coefficients of $x^2y$, we see that $a=\dfrac{3b}{2}.$

Now, since $f_y(-1,1) = 3$, we get \begin{align*} f_y(-1,1) &= 3 \\[3pt] b(-1)^3(1)+3(-1)^2+2 &= 3 \\[3pt] -b+3+2 &= 3 \\[3pt] b &= 2. \end{align*}

Finally, \[a=\dfrac{3b}{2}=3.\]

question.text: Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if \begin{align} f_x(x,y) &= ay^3e^{x-1}+3x^2e^{y-1}, \\[5pt] f_y(x,y) &= x^3e^{y-1}+3by^2e^{x-1}, \\[5pt] f_x(1,1) &= 4. \end{align}
question.explanation:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives: \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( f_x(x,y) \big) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( ay^3e^{x-1}+3x^2e^{y-1} \big) \\[3pt] &= 3ay^2e^{x-1}+3x^2e^{y-1} \\[7pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( f_y(x,y) \big)\\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( x^3e^{y-1}+3by^2e^{x-1}\big)\\[3pt] &= 3x^2e^{y-1}+3by^2e^{x-1} \end{align*}

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

\begin{align*} 3ay^2e^{x-1}+3x^2e^{y-1} =3x^2e^{y-1}+3by^2e^{x-1}. \end{align*}

Equating the coefficients of $y^2e^{x-1},$ respectively, we see that $a=b.$

Since $f_x(1,1)=4$, we get \begin{align*} f_x(1,1) &= 4 \\[3pt] a(1)^3e^{0}+3(1)^2e^{0}&= 4 \\[3pt] a+3 &= 4 \\[3pt] a&=1. \end{align*}

Finally, \[b = a =1.\]

question.text: Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if \begin{align} f_x(x,y) &= 2axy^2-4xy+15x, \\[5pt] f_y(x,y) &= bx^2y-2x^2-4y, \\[5pt] f_y(-1,-1) &= -5. \end{align}
question.explanation:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives: \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( f_x(x,y) \big) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( 2axy^2-4xy+15x \big) \\[5pt] &= 4axy-4x-0 \\[5pt] &= 4axy-4x \\[7pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( f_y(x,y) \big)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( bx^2y-2x^2-4y \big)\\[5pt] &= 2bxy - 4x - 0 \\[5pt] &= 2bxy - 4x \end{align*}

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

\begin{align*} 4axy-4x = 2bxy - 4x. \end{align*}

Equating the coefficients of $xy$, we see that $a=\dfrac{b}{2}.$

Now, since $f_y(-1,-1) = -5$, we get \begin{align*} f_x(-1,-1) &= -5 \\[5pt] b(-1)^2(-1)-2(-1)^2-4(-1) &= -5 \\[5pt] -b-2+4 &= -5 \\[5pt] b &= 7. \end{align*}

Finally, \[a=\dfrac{b}{2}=\dfrac{7}{2}.\]

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives

question.text:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

  1. $f_x(x,y)=x+3y$ and $f_y(x,y)=2e^y+3x$
  2. $f_x(x,y)=x^2 +e^x+y$ and $f_y(x,y)=2x+y^2+e^y$
  3. $f_x(x,y)=2y\sin{x}\cos{x}+xy+5$ and $f_y(x,y)=\sin^2{x}+xy-2$
question.explanation:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

  • For the first pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (x+3y) = 3 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (2e^y+3x) = 3. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the second pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big(x^2 +e^x+y \big)= 1 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big(2x+y^2+e^y \big)= 2. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) \ne f_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the third pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( 2y\sin{x}\cos{x}+xy+5 \big)= 2\sin{x}\cos{x}+x \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big(\sin^2{x}+xy-2 \big)=2\sin{x}\cos{x}+y. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y)\ne f_{yx}(x,y)$, the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I only'.

example.title: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives

question.text:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

  1. $f_x(x,y)=yx^2-4y$ and $f_y(x,y)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-4x$
  2. $f_x(x,y)=3-5x$ and $f_y(x,y)=1$
  3. $f_x(x,y)=3x^2+\sin{x}\sin{y}$ and $f_y(x,y)=\cos{x}\cos{y}-2y^3e^{y^2}$
question.explanation:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

  • For the first pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left(yx^2-4y\right) = x^2-4 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left(\dfrac{x^3}{3}-4x\right) = x^2-4. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the second pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (3-5x) = 0 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (1) = 0. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the third pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big(3x^2+\sin{x}\sin{y}\big) \\[3pt] &= 0 + \sin{x} \cdot \cos{y} \\[3pt] &= \sin{x}\cos{y} \\[7pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big(\cos{x}\cos{y}-2y^3e^{y^2}\big) \\[3pt] &= (- \sin{x}) \cdot \cos{y} - 0 \\[3pt] &=-\sin{x}\cos{y}. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y)\neq f_{yx}(x,y)$, the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only'.

question.text:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

  1. $f_x(x,y)=e^x\cos(e^x)$ and $f_y(x,y)=\sin(e^x)$
  2. $f_x(x,y)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ and $f_y(x,y)= \sqrt{1-y}$
  3. $f_x(x,y)=\ln(x^2+1)$ and $f_y(x,y)=x\ln(y^2+1)$
question.explanation:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

  • For the first pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (e^x\cos(e^x)) = 0 \\[5pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (\sin(e^x)) = e^x\cos(e^x). \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) \ne f_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the second pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big(\sqrt{1-x^2}\big)= 0 \\[5pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big(\sqrt{1-y}\big)=0. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the third pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big(\ln(x^2+1)\big)= 0 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big(x\ln(y^2+1) \big)= \ln(y^2+1). \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) \ne f_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

question.text:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

  1. $f_x(x,y)=x^3y-x$ and $f_y(x,y)=xy^3-y$
  2. $f_x(x,y)=e^{x+y}-2y$ and $f_y(x,y)=e^{x+y}-2x$
  3. $f_x(x,y)=\sqrt{x-1}$ and $f_y(x,y)=-3$
question.explanation:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

  • For the first pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left(x^3y-x\right) = x^3 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left(xy^3-y\right) = y^3. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) \neq f_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the second pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left(e^{x+y}-2y\right) = e^{x+y}-2 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left(e^{x+y}-2x\right) = e^{x+y}-2. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the third pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( \sqrt{x-1} \big) = 0\\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( -3 \big) = 0. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y)$, the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

question.text:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

  1. $f_x(x,y)=ye^x$ and $f_y(x,y)=e^x$
  2. $f_x(x,y)=2xe^{y+1}$ and $f_y(x,y)=x^2e^{y+1}$
  3. $f_x(x,y)=7x-3y$ and $f_y(x,y)=3x-7y$
question.explanation:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

  • For the first pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left(ye^x\right) = e^x \\[5pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left(e^x\right) = e^x. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the second pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left(2xe^{y+1}\right) = 2xe^{y+1} \\[5pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left(x^2e^{y+1}\right) = 2xe^{y+1}. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the third pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (7x-3y) = -3\\[5pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (3x-7y) = 3. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) \neq f_{yx}(x,y)$, the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

exampleAnswers.title: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point

question.text: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate $f_{xyx}(1,\pi)$ if $f_{xx}(x,y)=x^2 e^{xy} \cos{(xy)}.$
question.explanation:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

\begin{align*} f_{xyx}(x,y) & = f_{xxy}(x,y) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( f_{xx}(x,y) \big) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( x^2 e^{xy} \cos{(xy)} \big) \\[5pt] &= x^2 \left( xe^{xy} \cdot \cos(xy) + e^{xy} \cdot (-x\sin(xy))\right) \\[5pt] &= x^3 e^{xy} \left(\cos(xy) - \sin(xy)\right) . \end{align*}

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi,1)\mathbin{:}$

\[ f_{xyx}(1,\pi) = 1^3 e^{1 \cdot \pi} \left(\cos(1\cdot \pi) - \sin(1\cdot \pi)\right) = -e^{\pi} \]

example.title: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point

question.text: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate $f_{yxy}\left(6,\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ if $f_{xy}(x,y)=7+x\sin{y}.$
question.explanation:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

\begin{align*} f_{yxy}(x,y) & = f_{xyy}(x,y) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( f_{xy}(x,y) \big) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( 7+x\sin{y} \big) \\[5pt] &= x\cos{y}. \end{align*}

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $\left(6,\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\mathbin{:}$

\[ f_{yxy}\left(6,\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 6\cdot \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 3 \]

example.title: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point

question.text: Evaluate $f_{xyy}(2,2,2)$ given that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that \[ f_{yx}(x,y,z) = 2y\sqrt{\dfrac{z^3}{x}}+3z^3\sqrt{\dfrac{x}{y}} \]
question.explanation:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal.

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} f_{xyy}(x,y,z) & = f_{yxy}(x,y,z)\\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial y}\left(f_{yx}(x,y,z)\right)\\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial y}\left(2y\sqrt{\dfrac{z^3}{x}}+3z^3\sqrt{\dfrac{x}{y}}\right)\\[3pt] &=2\sqrt{\dfrac{z^3}{x}}+3z^3\sqrt{x}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y^3}}\right)\\[3pt] &=2\sqrt{\dfrac{z^3}{x}}-\dfrac{3}{2}z^3\sqrt{\dfrac{x}{y^3}}.\\[7pt] \end{align*}

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,2,2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} f_{xyy}(2,2,2) &=2\sqrt{\dfrac{(2)^3}{(2)}}-\dfrac{3}{2}(2)^3\sqrt{\dfrac{(2)}{(2)^3}}\\[3pt] &=2\cdot2-3\cdot 2\\[3pt] &=4-6\\[3pt] &=-2 \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point

question.text:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

\[ f_{zx}(x,y,z) = -\dfrac{2yz}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad f_{yz}(x,y,z) = \dfrac{2xz}{x^2+y^2} . \]

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,2,1)\mathbin{:}$

\[f_{zyy}(x,y,z) + f_{xxz}(x,y,z)\]
question.explanation:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal.

Hence, we have

\begin{align*} f_{zyy}(x,y,z) &= f_{yzy}(x,y,z)\\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial y}\left( f_{yz}(x,y,z) \right) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial y}\big( \dfrac{2xz}{x^2+y^2} \big) \\[3pt] &=-\dfrac{4xyz}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. \end{align*}

In addition, we have \begin{align*} f_{xxz}(x,y,z) &= f_{zxx}(x,y,z) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}\left( f_{zx}(x,y,z) \right) \\[3pt] &=\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}\left( -\dfrac{2yz}{x^2+y^2}\right) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{4xyz}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. \end{align*}

From the above, we get

\[f_{zyy}(x,y,z) + f_{xxz}(x,y,z)=-\dfrac{4xyz}{(x^2+y^2)^2}+\dfrac{4xyz}{(x^2+y^2)^2}=0.\]

Finally,

\[ f_{zyy}(1,2,1) + f_{xxz}(1,2,1)=0. \]

question.text: Consider that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first, second and third-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ What is the value of $f_{yx}(1,0) + f_{xyx}(1,0) - f_{xxy}(1,0)$ given that $f_{yx}(x,y)=2x\cos(xy)-x^2y\sin(xy)+1?$
question.explanation:
As the function and its first, second, and third-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ we must have $f_{xyx}(x,y)=f_{xxy}(x,y).$

Therefore, we can swap the order of the subscripts in the first term. This gives

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} f_{yx}(1,0) + f_{xyx}(1,0)-f_{xxy}(1,0) &= f_{yx}(1,0) + f_{xyx}(1,0) - f_{xyx}(1,0) \\[3pt] &= f_{yx}(1,0) + \cancel{f_{xxy}(1,0)} - \cancel{f_{xxy}(1,0)} \\[3pt] &= f_{yx}(1,0) \\[3pt] &= 2(1)\cos(1\cdot 0)-(1)^2(0)\sin(1\cdot 0)+1\\[3pt] &= 2 - 0 +1 \\[3pt] &=3. \end{align*}
